2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / moderate concern: Official IBGE Census (2000, 2010) and PNSB (2000, 2008) datasets have broad municipal coverage, but exact missingness and numeric cells in embedded table images (Tables 1-12) cannot be verified from the PDF text layer, and restricting the longitudinal analysis to continuously single-operator municipalities reduced sample counts from 67/128 (COPASA) and 346/284 (municipal) to 64 and 256 respectively.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Quantitative comparisons rely exclusively on unadjusted bivariate non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney U tests) with zero statistical control for baseline coverage ceiling effects, municipality size, socioeconomic status, macroeconomic conditions, the 2009 creation of regulator ARSAE, or federal non-repayable grants prioritizing small municipal utilities (all acknowledged qualitatively by the authors as major confounders).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: Accurately characterizes the institutional nature of COPASA's 2006 stock-market IPO (mixed-capital company remaining under majority state control while adopting capital-market governance and post-2009 ARSAE tariff regulation), reviewing state legislation, decrees, and corporate filings, though exact statute/decree citations are omitted and the 2000-2008/2010 quantitative window conflates six pre-IPO years with two-to-four post-IPO years.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Quantitative exposure measurement conflates pre-IPO (2000-2005) and post-IPO (2006-2008/2010) periods, PNSB survey protocols changed between 2000 and 2008 (affecting sewage comparability), and quantitative data on supply regularity, intermittence, and rationing were unavailable. Qualitative interviews were recorded and transcribed, though the semi-structured guide is not provided.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Draws on standard official administrative and census metrics (IBGE Census 2000/2010 household network and bathroom indicators, PNSB 2000/2008 water treatment volumes, Central Bank INPC/IPCA inflation vs COPASA tariff readjustments, and utility customer complaint records), but sewage comparability across PNSB waves was limited by protocol changes and operational continuity/intermittence relied solely on qualitative perceptions.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate / No pre-registration information: No pre-specified protocol or analysis plan is reported, and embedded raster tables/figures prevent inspection of exact test statistics in the extracted text stream; however, the authors transparently report null findings (e.g., non-significant differences at 95% confidence for bathrooms and sewage network connections) alongside significant differences.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: The longitudinal municipal comparison (64 COPASA vs 256 municipal operators) excludes over half of Minas Gerais's municipalities, omitting all localities with joint COPASA/municipal service and all municipalities newly acquired by COPASA after the 2006 IPO. Qualitative recruitment of 15 informants used purposive documentary and snowball sampling without reporting non-response or detailed participant counts in text (Table 1 rendered as an image).

domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its research objective: evaluating the consequences of COPASA's 2006 initial public offering (IPO) in Minas Gerais on water supply and sanitation service provision (coverage, universality, service quality, tariffs, and customer satisfaction) and assessing whether observed changes aligned with market interests or population needs.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining 2000-2012 official statistical and corporate series (IBGE PNSB 2000/2008, Demographic Census 2000/2010, Central Bank inflation series, COPASA annual/investor reports 2003-2012) with 15 semi-structured stakeholder interviews provides empirical data addressing both macro-level indicator trajectories and institutional mechanisms, despite pre/post timing limitations.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative exploratory/interpretive approach using semi-structured interviews with sector insiders is well suited to examine managerial incentives, regulatory dynamics, rural/small-town selectivity, and service-quality perceptions that official census indicators capture only indirectly.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Fifteen interactive semi-structured interviews were conducted with specialists, managers, and technicians across state policy, utility, regulatory, municipal, academic, and union bodies (acronyms ARSAE, FJP, COPASA, CMBH, COMUSA, UFMG, SENGE in text), recorded, and transcribed, though the interview guide and Table 1 cell text (embedded image) are not shown.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Transcribed interviews were systematically examined using content analysis (citing Bardin and Bauer) to identify recurring themes and discourse analysis (citing Rocha and Deusdara) to situate respondent statements within their institutional positions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Interpretations throughout the Results section are consistently supported by direct verbatim quotations attributed to anonymized institutional respondent codes (e.g., [ARSAE-03], [FJP-01], [COPASA-01], [COPASA-02], [COPASA-03], [CMBH], [COMUSA], [FJP-02], [UFMG], [SENGE]).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear methodological alignment connecting purposive/snowball recruitment of sector actors, semi-structured interviewing, content/discourse analysis, and thematic integration into the policy evaluation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the participants representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: To compare operator models longitudinally, the authors restricted the Minas Gerais municipal sample to localities continuously and exclusively served throughout 2000-2010 by COPASA (n = 64) or municipal entities (n = 256), excluding mixed-operator municipalities and all municipalities newly acquired during COPASA's post-2006 market expansion (where exclusive COPASA coverage rose from 67 to 128), making the panel unrepresentative of COPASA's full and expanding concession portfolio.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-5 (Methodology, pp. 252-253); PDF Pages 6-8 (Results, pp. 254-256)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are measurements appropriate regarding both the outcome and intervention (or exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Measuring COPASA's 2006 IPO via 2000-2008 (PNSB) and 2000-2010 (Census) differences conflates six pre-IPO years with two-to-four post-IPO years, preventing clean measurement of post-IPO exposure. In addition, the authors explicitly note protocol changes between the 2000 and 2008 PNSB surveys (especially for sewage) and the absence of quantitative indicators for supply regularity, intermittence, and rationing.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Methodology, p. 252); PDF Page 11 (Results, p. 259)

domain_ratings.justification: While official IBGE Census and PNSB surveys have broad state coverage, COPASA corporate series covered only 2003-2012, continuity/intermittence data were absent, and Tables 1-12 and Figures 1-8 are embedded as raster images not present in the PDF text layer, preventing verification of item-level completeness across municipalities.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Methodology, p. 252); PDF Pages 6-13 (Tables 2-12 and Figures 1-8, pp. 254-261)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the confounders accounted for in the design and analysis?
domain_ratings.justification: Quantitative inference relies solely on unadjusted paired Wilcoxon and independent Mann-Whitney U tests on raw 2000-2008/2010 differences, with no regression adjustment, matching, or stratification for baseline coverage ceiling effects, municipal size/income, federal grant programs targeting small municipal operators, or macroeconomic trends.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-5 (Methodology, pp. 252-253); PDF Pages 8-11, 14 (Results and Conclusions, pp. 256-259, 262)

domain_ratings.domain_name: During the study period, is the intervention administered (or exposure occurred) as intended?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the 64 vs 256 panel held operator identity constant across 2000-2010, the focal exposure (COPASA's 2006 IPO) was absent for the first six years of the 2000-2008/2010 observation window, and major concurrent co-interventions occurred unevenly across groups (federal non-repayable grants targeting small municipal utilities and the 2009 establishment of state regulator ARSAE).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3-5 (Introduction/Methodology, pp. 251-253); PDF Pages 8-9, 12 (Results, pp. 256-257, 260)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly justify combining statistical analysis of official/corporate indicators with semi-structured stakeholder interviews because available quantitative indicators could only indirectly capture service quality, managerial priorities, and institutional dynamics.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Quantitative comparisons (coverage, treatment technology, tariff adjustments vs inflation, complaint trends) and qualitative interview narratives are systematically woven together across every thematic subsection of Results rather than reported in isolated silos.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration directly strengthens substantive interpretation: qualitative insider accounts are used to contextualize quantitative patterns and caution against attributing statewide progress or differential growth rates solely to COPASA's IPO rather than federal funding and baseline disparities.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Apparent tensions—such as COPASA exhibiting higher absolute water coverage and treatment indicators yet slower 2000-2010 percentage gains than municipal operators, and meeting statutory water-quality standards while facing rising user complaints and dissatisfaction—are explicitly examined and explained through baseline conditions, federal grant targeting, tariff rigidity, and staff outsourcing.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Under MMAT 2018 criteria, while the qualitative and integration components are well executed (aside from absent researcher reflexivity), the quantitative non-randomized component suffers from unadjusted confounding, pre/post IPO timing conflation (2000-2008/2010 for a 2006 IPO), PNSB protocol shifts, and exclusion of switching/mixed municipalities.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Oliveira and Lima (2015) conduct a convergent mixed-methods empirical evaluation of the 2006 stock-market initial public offering (IPO) of Minas Gerais's state water and sanitation utility (COPASA), combining descriptive and non-parametric statistical analyses of official and corporate datasets (IBGE PNSB 2000 and 2008, Demographic Census 2000 and 2010, Central Bank inflation indices, and COPASA reports 2003-2012) with content and discourse analysis of 15 semi-structured interviews with sector managers, regulators, technicians, and specialists. Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018; Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative non-randomized 3.1-3.5, and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5), the study demonstrates strong qualitative coherence and thoughtful mixed-methods integration: qualitative evidence is systematically interwoven with indicator trends to explain institutional incentives, tariff pass-throughs, outsourcing problems, and why observed coverage changes cannot be naively attributed to the IPO. However, per MMAT 2018 guidance that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component, significant methodological limitations arise in the quantitative non-randomized component (3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 3.5 rated No; 3.3 Can't tell, noting also that Tables 1-12 and Figures 1-8 are embedded as unextracted raster images in the PDF): (1) comparing 2000 vs 2008/2010 outcomes conflates six pre-IPO years with only two-to-four post-IPO years; (2) restricting longitudinal Mann-Whitney U tests to municipalities continuously and exclusively operated by COPASA (n = 64) or municipal entities (n = 256) excludes over half the state's municipalities, including mixed-service systems and post-2006 expansion municipalities; (3) PNSB protocol changes between 2000 and 2008 impaired sewage comparability and continuity/intermittence metrics were unavailable; and (4) bivariate non-parametric tests make no statistical adjustment for baseline ceiling effects or federal non-repayable grant programs targeting smaller municipal utilities.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern in quantitative component (strong qualitative and integration components, but overall quality bounded by unadjusted non-randomized quantitative comparisons per MMAT 2018 guidance)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods empirical study combining a quantitative non-randomized longitudinal comparative analysis of official municipal water/sanitation indicators (2000-2010) and corporate/inflation series (2003-2012) with qualitative semi-structured interviews (n = 15) analyzed via content and discourse analysis
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aims and institutional background on PDF Pages 1-4 (pp. 249-252) and PDF Page 19 (Abstract); mixed-methods design, secondary datasets (COPASA 2003-2012, PNSB 2000/2008, IBGE Census 2000/2010), municipal sample restrictions (64 COPASA vs 256 municipal), Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney U tests, and qualitative interview sampling/analysis (n = 15) on PDF Pages 4-6 (Methodology, pp. 252-254); integrated quantitative-qualitative findings and measurement/confounding caveats on PDF Pages 6-14 (Results and Conclusions, pp. 254-262). Note: Tables 1-12 and Figures 1-8 were embedded as raster images in the source PDF so only their titles and sources appear in the text stream.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study collects, analyzes, and integrates both primary qualitative data (15 recorded semi-structured interviews analyzed via content and discourse analysis) and quantitative comparative observational data (paired Wilcoxon and independent Mann-Whitney U tests comparing 2000-2008/2010 municipal indicator changes between 64 COPASA and 256 municipal-operator localities, alongside corporate longitudinal series), fitting MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative non-randomized (3.1-3.5) module.
